gameOver.message: Player Gem25F Analyst is the winner

annotations.description: Playing Evolving Wilds instead of Command Tower means the Sol Ring will be cast off a tapped land (Evolving Wilds fetches a basic tapped), delaying Sol Ring by a turn. Command Tower enters untapped and produces colored mana, allowing the player to tap it for 1 mana to cast Sol Ring immediately on turn 1. With Evolving Wilds, the fetched land enters tapped, so Sol Ring can't be cast until turn 2. Getting Sol Ring down on turn 1 is a significant tempo advantage in Commander.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Evolving Wilds as the land for turn 1
annotations.betterLine: Play Command Tower (enters untapped, tap for 1 mana), then cast Sol Ring immediately on turn 1. Save Evolving Wilds for turn 2 when the tempo loss of a tapped land matters less.

annotations.description: Playing Forgotten Cave (which enters tapped) instead of a Mountain means Gem3F Libby has no mana available this turn. With Monologue Tax (2W) and Commander's Sphere (3) in hand, getting to 3 mana on turn 2 is important. Playing Mountain now would give 1 mana available this turn (though there's nothing to cast for 1 mana), but more importantly, playing Mountain turn 1 and then a tapped land (Forgotten Cave or Secluded Steppe) on turn 2 still yields 2 mana on turn 2. However, playing the tapped land first and Mountain second also yields 2 mana on turn 2. The real consideration is that Secluded Steppe produces white mana needed for Monologue Tax, while Forgotten Cave only produces red. With Osgir as commander (RW), the player needs white mana for Monologue Tax on turn 3. Playing Secluded Steppe (tapped, produces W) turn 1, then Mountain turn 2 gives R+W on turn 2, then another land turn 3 for potentially 3 mana including W for Monologue Tax. Playing Forgotten Cave turn 1 gives only R from it, meaning they'd need Secluded Steppe later (also tapped). Actually, the sequencing of tapped lands first is correct in principle, but Secluded Steppe would have been better than Forgotten Cave since it produces white mana needed for the commander and Monologue Tax. With two Mountains in hand already providing red, the white source is more valuable to deploy early.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Forgotten Cave (enters tapped, produces R) as turn 1 land drop.
annotations.betterLine: Play Secluded Steppe (enters tapped, produces W) as the turn 1 tapped land, preserving the option to play Mountain turn 2 for immediate red mana while having white available for Monologue Tax on turn 3.

annotations.description: Playing Rupture Spire on turn 2 with only one Forest means paying {1} to keep it requires tapping the Forest, leaving no mana available this turn. Azorius Chancery would have been better - it also enters tapped, but it bounces the Forest back to hand (which can be replayed next turn) and produces {W}{U} when it untaps, giving access to 3 colors without costing any mana. Alternatively, playing Plains or Forest would give an untapped land this turn, enabling Howling Mine (which costs {2}) next turn with two lands. Rupture Spire is the slowest option since it costs {1} just to keep and still enters tapped, effectively setting back tempo compared to Azorius Chancery which provides similar color fixing with better mana production.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Rupture Spire, which enters tapped and requires paying {1} from the only untapped Forest to not sacrifice it.
annotations.betterLine: Play Azorius Chancery, bouncing Forest to hand. Next turn, replay Forest untapped and have access to {W}{U} from Chancery plus {G} from Forest, enabling more plays including Oath of Druids or Howling Mine. This provides better color fixing and mana development without the {1} tax.

annotations.description: Cascade Bluffs as a turn 2 land drop is slightly suboptimal because it only produces colorless mana on its own and requires colored mana input to function. Command Tower always produces colored mana unconditionally and is the stronger early land drop. Both accomplish the immediate goal of casting Spellbinding Soprano, but Command Tower provides better flexibility in future turns.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Cascade Bluffs as turn 2 land drop
annotations.betterLine: Play Command Tower, which unconditionally produces any color in the commander's identity, and save Cascade Bluffs for a later turn when more colored sources are available to feed it.

annotations.description: Haiku ESPN activated Cascade Bluffs for colorless mana to cast Spellbinding Soprano, but Soprano costs {1}{R}. They have Smoldering Marsh (untapped) which can produce {R}, and Cascade Bluffs which can produce {U/R} + {T} for {U}{U}, {U}{R}, or {R}{R}, or just {C}. To cast Soprano ({1}{R}), they need one red and one generic. The optimal line is to tap Smoldering Marsh for {R} and Cascade Bluffs for {C}, which is exactly what they did — Smoldering Marsh provides the {R} and Cascade Bluffs the {1}. Actually, this is correct since they need to keep colored mana available... wait, they're tapping out either way with only 2 lands. Tapping Cascade Bluffs for {C} and Smoldering Marsh for {R} is fine. However, tapping Cascade Bluffs for {U}{R} (paying {U/R}) would give them {U}{R} from Bluffs and {B} or {R} from Smoldering Marsh — but that wastes mana since Soprano only costs {1}{R}. The colorless option is actually the most efficient here since it avoids spending an extra blue or red mana from the filter ability. This is correct play.
annotations.actionTaken: Activated Cascade Bluffs for {C}
annotations.betterLine: This was actually the correct activation

annotations.description: Played Plains instead of Command Tower. Command Tower produces any color in the commander's color identity, making it strictly more flexible than a basic Plains. With Propaganda (needs U) and Cataclysmic Gearhulk (needs WW) in hand, having maximum color flexibility now is better. Plains can be played on a future turn when the extra flexibility of Command Tower matters less.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Plains as land for turn 2
annotations.betterLine: Play Command Tower instead, saving the basic Plains for a later turn when color flexibility matters less

annotations.description: Playing an untapped land (Plains) on turn 2 when there's nothing to spend 1 mana on this turn, while holding Secluded Steppe (a tapped land) that will cost tempo later. Standard sequencing says play tapped lands when you can't use the mana anyway.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Plains (untapped) on turn 2 with no 1-mana plays available
annotations.betterLine: Play Secluded Steppe (enters tapped) on turn 2 to get the tapped land out of the way, preserving Plains for a turn where having untapped mana immediately matters more

annotations.description: Playing Forest instead of Azorius Chancery is suboptimal. Azorius Chancery would bounce Rupture Spire (which costs {1} to keep anyway and enters tapped) or Forest back to hand, and next turn would provide {W}{U} mana, giving access to white and blue mana alongside the existing green. Playing Forest only adds another green source. With Oath of Druids ({1}{G}) castable this turn using Forest + Rupture Spire regardless of land drop choice, the question is what sets up future turns better. Azorius Chancery would give access to {W}{U} next turn, enabling Howling Mine + holding up Swords to Plowshares, while Forest just gives redundant green mana. However, Azorius Chancery enters tapped and bounces a land, so it temporarily reduces available mana. The reasoning mentions wanting to cast Oath of Druids this turn, which Forest enables alongside Rupture Spire - but Azorius Chancery entering tapped wouldn't prevent this since the existing two lands (Forest already on board + Rupture Spire) can still cast Oath. Playing Azorius Chancery (bouncing Rupture Spire to replay later, avoiding the {1} tax) while casting Oath with the two untapped lands would have been slightly better sequencing for future mana development.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Forest as land drop
annotations.betterLine: Play Azorius Chancery (bouncing Rupture Spire to avoid its drawback), then cast Oath of Druids with the two untapped lands (Forest + the other). This develops better mana fixing for future turns with access to white and blue.

annotations.description: Howling Mine gives all opponents extra cards, which is a significant cost in a 4-player game. With only 3 opponents having minimal board presence on turn 3, giving everyone extra draws accelerates opponents more than it helps Sonnet Timmy. Oath of Druids would have been a stronger play since Sonnet Timmy controls no creatures while Haiku ESPN has Spellbinding Soprano on the battlefield, meaning Oath would immediately trigger for Sonnet Timmy on their next upkeep to cheat a creature into play. Additionally, the reasoning mentions casting both spells this turn, but with only 3 lands (one being Rupture Spire which produces any color), they could cast Oath of Druids (1G) with Forest + Rupture Spire and still have Forest left, but couldn't cast both. Oath of Druids is a much higher-impact card that directly benefits the caster asymmetrically.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Howling Mine, giving all four players extra card draw symmetrically.
annotations.betterLine: Cast Oath of Druids instead, which would trigger on Sonnet Timmy's upkeep since Haiku ESPN controls a creature (Spellbinding Soprano) and Sonnet Timmy controls none, allowing them to cheat a creature into play from their library.

annotations.description: Playing a basic Island when Command Tower or Grixis Panorama would be strictly better. Command Tower taps for any color in a Grixis (UBR) deck, providing more flexible mana. Grixis Panorama can fetch any basic Island/Swamp/Mountain later. With Cascade Bluffs and Smoldering Marsh already providing UR colors, the player needs black mana most urgently (for Sever the Bloodline and Anhelo). Command Tower would provide that flexibility, and Darkwater Catacombs or Thriving Moor would also help fix for black. Playing a basic Island is the least useful land since blue is already well-covered by Cascade Bluffs.
annotations.actionTaken: Played basic Island as land drop for the turn.
annotations.betterLine: Play Command Tower to have access to any color (especially black for Sever the Bloodline and Anhelo), or play Thriving Moor (choosing blue or red) to fix black mana while keeping Command Tower for a future turn when multiple colors are needed.

annotations.description: Playing Plains instead of Command Tower wastes flexibility. Command Tower produces any color in the commander's identity (at least WUB), making it strictly better than Plains for an untapped land drop. Playing Command Tower now preserves the basic Plains for later, where basics have advantages (fetchable, immune to nonbasic hate). The player's reasoning about 'paying for Phantom Steed' is also confused since Phantom Steed is already on the battlefield.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Plains as their land drop for turn 3.
annotations.betterLine: Play Command Tower instead, preserving the basic Plains for a future land drop where being a basic is relevant.

annotations.description: Casting Monologue Tax before playing a land is a sequencing error. Gem3F Libby has Secluded Steppe and Plains in hand, and only 3 lands on the battlefield. Playing a land first (Plains) would allow casting Commander's Sphere instead, which provides mana acceleration and card draw potential. Alternatively, playing the land first is simply correct sequencing - you should always play your land before casting spells in case you draw into something or need the information. More importantly, Commander's Sphere would ramp them toward their expensive cards (Duplicant at 6, Hellkite Tyrant at 6) while Monologue Tax is a relatively low-impact enchantment in multiplayer that only triggers on opponents' second spells each turn.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Monologue Tax for 2W using all three lands, without first making a land drop.
annotations.betterLine: Play Plains first (making a land drop), then cast Commander's Sphere for 3 mana to accelerate toward the powerful 6-drops in hand (Duplicant, Hellkite Tyrant). Monologue Tax could be played next turn.

annotations.description: Playing Azorius Chancery on turn 4 loses tempo by entering tapped and bouncing a land, when Plains would provide more available mana this turn. With Plains, Timmy would have 4 untapped lands after casting Oath of Druids, keeping {W} open for Swords to Plowshares as interaction. With Chancery, after bouncing a land and casting Oath, there's minimal mana left open.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Azorius Chancery, which enters tapped and bounces a land, reducing available mana this turn.
annotations.betterLine: Play Plains (enters untapped), then cast Oath of Druids with Forest+Forest/Rupture Spire, keeping Plains untapped for Swords to Plowshares as potential interaction. Save Azorius Chancery for a later turn when the tempo loss matters less.

annotations.description: Returned Azorius Chancery to hand with its own ETB trigger, effectively wasting the entire land drop this turn. The player ends up with the same board state as before playing the land, losing a full turn of development.
annotations.actionTaken: Returned Azorius Chancery (the bounce land itself) to hand, netting zero lands played this turn.
annotations.betterLine: Return a Forest to hand instead, keeping Azorius Chancery on the battlefield for WU mana production. This would provide better color fixing for Swords to Plowshares (W) and Reins of Power (2UU) in hand, and the Forest could simply be replayed next turn.

annotations.description: Oath of Druids triggers at each player's upkeep, allowing a player who controls fewer creatures than an opponent to reveal cards until they find a creature. Sonnet Timmy currently controls 0 creatures while Gem25F Analyst has Phantom Steed and Wayfarer's Bauble (Phantom Steed is a creature), and Haiku ESPN has Spellbinding Soprano. However, Oath of Druids benefits ALL players symmetrically - any opponent with fewer creatures than another opponent can also use it. In a 4-player game, this is extremely risky as it helps opponents cheat creatures into play too. Additionally, Sonnet Timmy should consider playing the land (Azorius Chancery or Homeward Path) before casting spells to have more mana available and better sequencing. The Azorius Chancery entering tapped means it should be played sooner rather than later. Playing the land first is generally correct sequencing.

annotations.description: Haiku ESPN's commander is Anhelo, the Painter (UBR colors). Thriving Moor enters tapped and provides black plus one chosen color, but the reasoning says 'green and white mana for flexibility' which is wrong - Anhelo's color identity is UBR, so the chosen color should be blue or red. More importantly, Choked Estuary would likely be the better choice here. Haiku ESPN has an Island in hand (none visible, but has blue sources) and could potentially reveal a Swamp or Island to have Choked Estuary enter untapped on a future turn. However, looking at their hand, they don't have a Swamp or Island card to reveal, so Choked Estuary would enter tapped anyway. The real issue is that Thriving Moor also enters tapped, and both provide black mana, but Choked Estuary provides UB (both needed colors) while Thriving Moor provides B + one chosen color. Since Haiku ESPN already has Darkwater Catacombs (UB), Cascade Bluffs (UR), Command Tower, and Rakdos Signet (BR), the mana base is relatively covered. The choice between the two is close, but the reasoning given is completely wrong about 'green and white mana' which suggests confused decision-making.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose Thriving Moor to put onto the battlefield, with reasoning about 'green and white mana flexibility' despite being in UBR colors.
annotations.betterLine: Either land is defensible since both enter tapped, but Choked Estuary provides both U and B from a single land without needing to pay 1 like Darkwater Catacombs, making it slightly more efficient for casting Mystic Confluence or other UU spells in hand.

annotations.description: Haiku ESPN should play Choked Estuary first before casting any spell. More importantly, casting Rite of the Raging Storm before playing a land is a sequencing error - land should always come first. Additionally, Rite of the Raging Storm gives every player a 5/1 token each turn, which is problematic when Haiku ESPN is at only 24 life (the lowest life total). While the Lightning Ragers can't attack Haiku ESPN, they give opponents free 5-power attackers to direct at each other or trigger effects. Izzet Signet would have been a better play to ramp, followed by holding up Mystic Confluence as interaction, especially given the low life total and need to be defensive.

annotations.betterLine: Play Choked Estuary first, then cast Izzet Signet for ramp, and hold up mana for Mystic Confluence as a defensive option given the dangerously low 24 life total.

annotations.description: With Gem3F Libby at only 3 life and Rite of the Raging Storm on the battlefield (which creates a 5/1 Lightning Rager for each player at the beginning of their upkeep), Libby is likely dead soon anyway. However, casting Propaganda ({2}{U}) would provide important protection against the Lightning Rager tokens from Rite of the Raging Storm, which threaten 5 damage per turn from each opponent. With 40 life, this isn't immediately critical, but Propaganda is a strong defensive permanent that gets better the longer it's in play. Wall of Omens replaces itself and provides a 0/4 blocker, which is reasonable, but Propaganda would tax all opponents' attacks going forward. The decision is close - Wall of Omens cantrips and blocks, while Propaganda provides broader protection. Additionally, casting Wall of Omens before combat with Sefris as commander (W/U/B) could be relevant for dungeon venturing if Sefris were in play, but she appears to be in the command zone. The play is defensible since the cantrip digs for answers.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Wall of Omens for {1}{W} to draw a card and get a 0/4 blocker
annotations.betterLine: Cast Propaganda for {2}{U} to tax attackers, particularly the 5/1 Lightning Rager tokens from Rite of the Raging Storm that threaten significant damage each turn cycle

annotations.description: Gem3F Libby is at 2 life. Sonnet Timmy has Treacherous Terrain in hand, which deals damage to each opponent equal to the number of lands they control. Libby controls 8 lands (Forgotten Cave, Plains, Mountain, Plains, Plains, Plains + Monologue Tax and Thousand-Year Elixir are not lands). Actually counting lands: Forgotten Cave, Plains, Mountain, Plains, Plains, Plains = 6 lands minimum. That's 6 damage to Libby who is at 2 life - lethal. Treacherous Terrain costs {6}{R}{G} and Sonnet Timmy has Forest (untapped), Plains (untapped), Homeward Path (untapped) available plus tapped lands. Looking at untapped lands: Forest, Plains, Homeward Path = only 3 mana available with untapped lands. The tapped lands can't produce mana. So Timmy only has 3 mana available and Treacherous Terrain costs 8. Wait - but it's listed as a choice, meaning the game engine determined it was castable. Let me re-check. The choices include Treacherous Terrain {6}{R}{G} as castable. If the game is offering it, Timmy must have enough mana. Looking more carefully at the board - many lands are tapped but some are untapped: Forest (untapped), Plains (untapped), Homeward Path (untapped). That's only 3 mana. But wait, the game engine is offering it as a legal cast option, so perhaps I'm misreading the tapped status. If it's castable, declining to cast it when an opponent is at 2 life is a major blunder - it would eliminate Libby.
